_: Kindred projects: who else shows the planet's daily state on a globe or a map, with what data and under what licence. Written by hand 2026-09-08 after checking each licence at the source; keys: name, url, code (repository or null), licence (of the code), what, data, why (what we can take from it), kind (app | library).

items.name: earth.nullschool.net
items.what: Wind, ocean currents, waves, temperature and aerosols drawn as moving particles on a rotating globe, updated every three hours.
items.data: GFS forecasts (US National Weather Service), ocean from OSCAR and WaveWatch, aerosols from GEOS-5 and CAMS; coastlines from Natural Earth.
items.why: The reference for animating flow: particles carried by the wind field. The whole app is MIT, so its projection and particle code can be reused with attribution; the live site itself is a personal project by Cameron Beccario, not a service to embed.

items.name: Climate Pulse (Copernicus C3S)
items.licence: site: not open source; data under the Copernicus licence (free use with attribution)
items.what: Daily and monthly global air temperature and sea surface temperature since 1979 as a map and a globe, anomalies against 1991–2020, works on a phone.
items.data: ERA5 reanalysis for air, ERA5 SST; daily from 2023, monthly and annual from 1979.
items.why: The cleanest public-facing presentation of exactly our two headline series. Not code to reuse, but the standard to measure ourselves against.

items.name: Globe Viz, daily sea surface temperature
items.what: Daily OISST since 1982 on a rotating globe, absolute and anomaly, with a time slider.
items.data: NOAA OISST v2.1 daily, 0.25° grid, downloaded and pre-processed into HDF tiles.
items.why: Same data we already read box by box; shows the pipeline from OISST grid to a globe in the browser, MIT-licensed end to end.

items.name: Fluid Earth (Byrd Polar, Ohio State)
items.what: A WebGL viewer of the atmosphere and oceans over time, light enough for phones and slow connections, built for education and outreach.
items.data: GFS, GEOS, OSCAR, RTGSST and others, served as pre-tiled fields.
items.why: The closest open engine to what a bridge42worlds globe would need: layers, time, low bandwidth; maintained by a university centre.

items.name: A century of surface temperature anomalies (Google experiment)
items.licence: WebGL Globe component under Apache 2.0 (Google Data Arts); repository itself carries that licence file
items.what: Yearly surface temperature anomalies since 1880 as bars on a WebGL globe.
items.why: The bar-on-globe idiom for a long annual record; small and readable code.

items.name: globe.gl
items.what: A web component for data layers on a three-dimensional globe: points, arcs, polygons, heatmaps, tiles, labels, on ThreeJS and WebGL.
items.data: Any: the caller supplies coordinates and values.
items.why: The quickest path to our own globe: Niño boxes, regional boxes, moorings and satellite footprints are all points and polygons; SST and rain grids can go on as heatmap or tile layers.

items.name: CesiumJS
items.what: A full three-dimensional globe and map engine with terrain, imagery, time-dynamic data and a camera, in the browser without plugins.
items.data: Any; imagery and terrain from Cesium ion or your own tiles.
items.why: The heavy option if the globe ever needs terrain, precise geodesy or time-dynamic layers beyond what globe.gl handles; more to learn and to load.

items.name: WebGL Globe (Google Data Arts)
items.what: The original small Chrome Experiments globe: bars of data on a textured sphere, a few hundred lines.
items.why: Where the bar-globe idiom came from; good for understanding before choosing a bigger library.
